audits.claim: Solís et al. (2020) publisher abstract reports 991-1147 cal AD (ABA cleaning) versus 1159-1261 cal AD (Soxhlet plus ABA), with the authors preferring the latter; these are treatment-dependent support dates, not painting dates.
audits.source_locator: Crossref work record for doi:10.1017/RDC.2020.71, JATS 'abstract' field, Radiocarbon 62(6):1543-1550; identical abstract text independently reconstructed from the OpenAlex work record abstract_inverted_index (https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1017/RDC.2020.71)
audits.source_excerpt: placed the age of the bark paper between 991 and 1147 cal AD ... resulted in younger ages, between 1159 and 1261 cal AD
audits.retrieval_method: curl to public scholarly REST APIs (Crossref work record carrying the publisher-deposited abstract; OpenAlex abstract_inverted_index reconstruction as an independent second copy of the same publisher text); raw JSON saved under reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round5-08/rdc2020-crossref.json and rdc2020-openalex.json. The Cambridge Core publisher page itself still returned HTTP 429 (also via the FetchURL tool) and was not read; Unpaywall reports the article closed (no OA copy); no paywall bypass attempted.
audits.basis: The publisher-deposited abstract confirms every element of the claim verbatim: ABA-only results 'placed the age of the bark paper between 991 and 1147 cal AD'; 'The second cleaning method with Soxhlet plus ABA, resulted in younger ages, between 1159 and 1261 cal AD'; and the stated preference for the latter — 'we consider that when Sohxlet [sic] is used as part of the cleaning protocol, organic contaminants are reduced to a minimum, and 14C dates are more reliable.' The abstract itself scopes both ranges to the support ('the age of the bark paper'; 'the vegetal support of the MCM belongs to Postclassical Mayan period'), matching the claim's 'treatment-dependent support dates, not painting dates' framing without over-extension. Two independent aggregator copies of the same deposited text agree word-for-word, so the reading does not rest on a single source; but this is abstract-level confirmation only.
audits.coupling_implication: For the entry's design handoff the era coupling is support-level: the two calibrated ranges bracket the bark support between roughly the late tenth and mid-thirteenth centuries while the abstract assigns the codex's Venus-cycle content to the Postclassic horizon; painted content, use history, and any later additions must not be frozen to either range, and the entry's instruction not to treat the INAH announcement range (1021-1154/1152) as a timeless consensus stands unchanged.
audits.limits: Abstract-level confirmation only: Cambridge Core remained HTTP 429 this pass, the article is closed access (Unpaywall oa_status 'closed'), and the full text — probability distributions, calibration curve, laboratory/sample details — remains uninspected, so the entry's (to-verify) flags on the 2020 article and on the 2018 chapter are not upgraded. The deposited abstract carries a printed 'Sohxlet' typo, quoted here verbatim.

audits.claim: Madrid codex: the analytical study [MAD] places it in the Late Postclassic, probably the second half of the fifteenth century — a study estimate, not a secure colophon date.
audits.source_locator: Internet Archive snapshot 2023-09-08 of the ScienceDirect article page (title and author list match Buti et al., 'Non-invasive investigation of a pre-Hispanic Maya screenfold book: the Madrid Codex', JAS 42:166-178), article introduction paragraph p0050 as embedded in the Elsevier article JSON and mirrored in the rendered page
audits.source_excerpt: most scholars today agree that the codex is a Late Postclassic Maya manuscript, probably painted during the second half of the 15th century in north-eastern Yucatan
audits.retrieval_method: Live ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 (also via FetchURL); Crossref, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar all carry no abstract for doi:10.1016/j.jas.2013.08.008 (publisher elision at S2), Unpaywall reports closed, Europe PMC zero hits. OpenAIRE search exposed four institutional instances (IRIS CNR hdl 20.500.14243/258347; Perugia AIR hdl 11391/1219689; Bologna AIR hdl 11585/261279; CNR ExploRA publications.cnr.it/doc/289094), all behind Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenges — left unresolved, no bypass. Wayback CDX then showed two snapshots of the publisher page; the 2023-09-08 snapshot (HTTP 200) was fetched with curl and its raw HTML saved under reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round5-08/wb-sd-buti.html. This is the publisher's own free-to-view article page read from a public archive, not a paywall circumvention.
audits.basis: The study's own introduction states: 'Despite the fact that the dating and provenance of the Madrid Codex had been the subject of a long-standing discussion, most scholars today agree that the codex is a Late Postclassic Maya manuscript, probably painted during the second half of the 15th century in north-eastern Yucatan.' This confirms the claimed placement and dating horizon, and the sentence's own hedging ('most scholars today agree', 'probably', introduced by a record of long-standing discussion) directly matches the claim's 'study estimate, not a secure colophon date' framing — no colophon or secure date is asserted. The same paragraph also supports the entry's manufacture-versus-later-use caution: it cites a reading of the Latin/Spanish text on the page-56 paper patch suggesting use in the same region 'until the first decade of the 17th century', and calls the codex 'a compilation of information drawn from different sources across time and space'. The article abstract itself names only materials (calcium carbonate, red ochre, vegetal carbon black, Maya blue) and no date, so the dating evidence retrieved here sits in the introduction, consistent with the entry's 'publisher introduction and conclusions' attribution as far as re-inspected.
audits.coupling_implication: Era/dress coupling stays estimate-level: a Late Postclassic, second-half-fifteenth-century painting horizon for a Yukatek screenfold whose compilation draws from sources across time and space and whose documented use extends into the early seventeenth century — so costume, iconography, and calendrical content in any design record must not be pinned to a single dated moment, and the entry's demand to distinguish manufacture from later colonial use is reinforced by the study's own text.
audits.limits: Read from the Internet Archive snapshot (2023-09-08) of the publisher page because the live page returns HTTP 403; only the abstract and the introduction-preview paragraphs were retrieved — the conclusions section of the article was not reached in the snapshot, so the entry's 'introduction and conclusions' locus is re-verified at the introduction's dating sentence only. The repository copies surfaced by OpenAIRE are Cloudflare-challenged, search engines (DuckDuckGo anomaly wall, Mojeek automated-query block) and Scilit (Akamai access denied) were unusable without bypass attempts, and scholar.archive.org/fatcat were unreachable from this network; none of these affect the publisher-page reading but bound how far the corroboration could be pushed. The SLUB institutional 'around 1500' estimate noted in the prior ledger remains a distinct, non-identical estimate; no correction to either is warranted.
